newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-CEO quits as D.Babcock announces loss.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-CEO quits as D.Babcock announces loss.

text.p: Troubled German engineering group Deutsche Babcock AG said on Monday that chief executive Heyo Schmiedeknecht resigned after the company slid to a loss and suffered negative cash flow in the 1995/96 business year.
Schmiedeknecht, at the helm since 1990, will be replaced from February 1 by Klaus Lederer, the 48-year-old head of ITT Automotive Europe, a unit of ITT Industries Inc.
Deutsche Babcock said in a regulatory statement that its supervisory board accepted Schmiedeknecht's resignation, but gave no reason.

But the departure of Schmiedeknecht, 57, had been widely expected in Germany's weekend press after his bid to restructure the group failed to improve the bottom line. He had been blamed for buying companies that had turned into loss makers.

The statement also said that Lederer, who has also been worldwide general manager of ITT Automotive Corp., would bring "an international dimension" to Deutsche Babcock's business when he takes over at the end of January.

News of the management change came late in the day and analysts were not immediately available to comment. But Babcock shares had risen during the trading day on investor hopes of a management change. The share ended up 4.50 marks at 69 marks.

Deutsche Babcock said that, in the year to September 30, 1996, the company slid to a group net loss of 434 million marks after a 46 million mark profit in the previous year. The company last October estimated losses would at 400 million marks.
Group sales rose to 8.7 billion marks from 8.3 billion, but incoming orders were down to 8.4 billion from 9.8 billion.
Cash flow plunged to a negative 279 million marks after a positive 251 million marks the year before.

Pressure on Schmiedeknecht to step down had been mounting after he admitted last October the company faced a liquidity shortage of 100 million marks -- on top of a 600 million mark credit line agreed with banks in mid-1996.
At that time Babcock had rejected growing speculation that it was insolvent and said its core plant and engineering businesses would be profitable in 1995/96, despite losses in non-core operations.

The reorganisation was expected to include the sale of 20 of the company's 60 subsidiaries, but analysts said at the time that the efforts were proceeding too slowly and restructuring charges were likely to be higher than expected.
